newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus fall eases pressure on government.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus fall eases pressure on government.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus continued to shrink last year to the relief of the government, but economists warned Monday that the surplus may start growing soon, as feared by the United States.

The government said the surplus in the current account, which measures trade in both goods and services, fell 30.9 percent to 7.18 trillion yen ($58.3 billion) in 1996, marking three consecutive years of declines.
"The surplus is still on a declining trend, but it may start rising again from around the middle of the year," said Tomoko Fujii, an economist at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd.
In December alone, the current account surplus fell 23.1 percent from a year earlier to 820.7 billion yen ($6.67 billion), largely in line with economists' expectations.

The merchandise trade surplus for the whole of 1996 fell 26.2 percent from the previous year to 9.1152 trillion yen ($74.1 billion) and in December it shrank 20.0 percent to 1.046 trillion yen ($8.5 billion).
"Both the current account figures for December and 1996 have declined and that trend should continue for some time," a Ministry of Finance official told reporters.
The data had no immediate impact on the currency markets, which were more concerned about the outcome of the Group of Seven meeting over the weekend.

In a statement released after their meeting on Saturday, the G7 nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- signalled their desire for stability in currency markets by saying that their currencies were no longer out of sync with economic reality.
The United States indicated during the G7 meeting that it was concerned about possible growth in Japan's trade surplus, which has been a source of friction between the two countries.

Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Monday that Japan told U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin during talks on the sidelines of the G7 meeting that its current account surplus was still on a declining trend. "I told him that I did not think the current account balance was worsening as is viewed in the United States," Mitsuzuka said.

Shunsuke Motani, an economist at Sphynx Investment Research, said the weakness in the yen against the dollar boosted the value of imports, which made it appear as though the surplus was still declining, despite a drop in volume.
He said December customs-cleared trade data released at the end of January showed imports rose 13.4 percent in value terms while volume fell 2.6 percent.

"Once the drop in the yen stops, it (growth in surplus) will appear (on official data). I don't think it'll appear in February or March data, but maybe in April data to be announced in May or June," Motani said.

Other economists said the yen's fall had made Japanese products more price competitive abroad, which in turn had contributed to a rise in exports. They said this would gradually halt the declining trend of the current account surplus.
"Exports, especially of cars, are rising from the impact of the weak yen and firm demand in the United States," said Hiroshi Suzuki, an economist at Norinchukin Research Institute.

A weak yen boosts exports and so gives the economy a lift, but too steep a drop could undermine shaky Tokyo share prices and later lead to an equally steep and unwelcome rise in the Japanese currency.
